newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Latam arms spending may rise, but risk of race low.
newsitem.headline: Latam arms spending may rise, but risk of race low.

text.p: Washington's decision to lift a 20-year ban on the sale of high-tech weaponry to Latin America is likely to increase military spending in the region, but officials say it should not trigger an arms race.

After U.S. officials announced President Bill Clinton's reversal of the ban last Friday, Lima newspaper El Comercio carried a cartoon of Uncle Sam showing Latin America a sign saying "Arms For Sale." The caption read: "Dangerous Offer!"

The cartoon sums up long-held fears that the resumption of sophisticated weapons sales, banned under the Carter administration when much of the region was under military rule, could threaten its new-found stability and democracy.

Two countries as far flung as Mexico and Paraguay voiced such concerns on Monday when presidents Ernesto Zedillo and Juan Carlos Wasmosy vowed to adopt "control measures on the purchase of sophisticated attack weapons which could, eventually, promote an arms race in the region."
Peru's recent purchase of a squadron of MiG-29 fighters from eastern Europe and Chile's interest in buying U.S. F-16 jets appear to underline such a threat.

Argentine military analyst Rosendo Fraga believes the U.S. policy turn "could contribute to increasing military spending" in the region that has the lowest arms expenditure as a percentage of economic output.

In a potent symbol of how Latin America has tamed the men in uniform who once ruled by terror, Fraga said it spends 1.94 percent of gross domestic product on weaponry compared to 3.7 in developed democracies and 9.06 percent in the Middle East.
Officers and analysts acknowledge the ban helped stabilise Latin America, which U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff head Gen. John Shalikashvili called a "dream come true" on a recent tour.

Some analysts see a contradiction in the U.S. issuing what Fraga called "political support for Latin America countries to rearm" mere weeks after the U.S. envoy to Peru, Dennis Jett, criticised Peru for spending on MiGs, not schools, and warned Lima: "This could now lead to an arms race."

Analysts say resumed sales from U.S. makers desperate for new markets since the end of the Cold War were inevitable after Peru went shopping in Eastern Europe and Chile started looking at French Mirage-2000s and Swiss Grippens, since it could not buy the U.S. F-16s it really wanted.
But Latin American leaders believe they have created enough mutual trust to avoid an all-out regional arms race.
"The best plan for national defence is getting on with your neighbours," said Argentine President Carlos Menem.
Brazilian Foreign Minister Luiz Felipe Lampreia said his country was unworried "because conditions in Latin America are not likely to prompt an arms race."

In Chile, the area's biggest military shopper spending 2.55 percent of GDP on arms compared to less than one percent in Argentina and Brazil, Defence Minister Edmundo Perez Yoma spoke of "transparency" and "measures of mutual confidence."

The long border between Chile and Argentina nearly sparked a war in 1978. When regional defence chiefs met in Argentina in October 1996, Argentina was cautious about resuming U.S. arms sales because of the spending imbalance with Chile.
But Argentina, whose military apologised in 1995 for the kidnaps and murders of its 1976-83 regime, is now planning joint exercises with Chile in 1998 in Argentina.

"We see no risk of an arms race," said one Argentine officer, pointing to pacts with Brazil and Chile for prior warning of arms purchases. "It's not asking permission, it shows we're acting with total transparency to build trust."
